import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score
from _common_en import DATASET, METRIQUES, SERIE, MUET, READING, BENCHMARKS, YES_NO, lire, tableau

c = lire("modele_horizons.csv")
HORIZONS = {"sens": [1, 5, 20, 60, 120], "vol": [5, 20, 60, 120]}


def points_ic(t, series, titre, axe_y):
    """Gap to the benchmark and 99.4% interval, one point per horizon and per series."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    n = len(series)
    for k, (nom, (filtre, couleur)) in enumerate(series.items()):
        x = t[filtre]
        pos = [HORIZONS_POS[h] + (k - (n - 1) / 2) * 0.18 for h in x["horizon"]]
        fig.add_scatter(x=pos, y=x["ecart"], mode="markers", name=nom,
                        marker=dict(size=10, color=couleur, line=dict(width=2, color="white")),
                        error_y=dict(type="data", symmetric=False, array=x["ic_haut"] - x["ecart"],
                                     arrayminus=x["ecart"] - x["ic_bas"], color=couleur, thickness=2, width=4),
                        customdata=np.stack([x["horizon"], x["ic_bas"], x["ic_haut"]], axis=1),
                        hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>Horizon %{{customdata[0]}} sessions<br>Gap %{{y:+.3f}}"
                                      "<br>99.4% CI: %{customdata[1]:+.3f} to %{customdata[2]:+.3f}<extra></extra>")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=MUET, width=1.5, dash="dot"))
    fig.update_layout(title=titre, height=400, yaxis_title=axe_y,
                      xaxis=dict(tickvals=list(HORIZONS_POS.values()), ticktext=[f"{h} sessions" for h in HORIZONS_POS]))
    return fig

title: Results: the model versus the benchmark
text:
In brief
A machine learning model was trained to forecast cocoa from the 8 factor families. It was compared with simple models without any factor, which only look at the past price. If the factors carried information, the model should beat these simple models. It does not, at any horizon.
A few terms:

Price direction: will the price be higher or lower in 1, 5, 20, 60 or 120 sessions? A session is a trading day: 20 sessions are about a month, 120 about six months.
Balanced accuracy: the share of correct forecasts, corrected so that rises and falls weigh equally. 0.5 corresponds to chance, like a coin toss.
Volatility: the size of price moves, whether up or down. It is measured by the RMSE, the average forecast error: the lower, the better.
Benchmark: the best model without factors, for example “the recent trend continues” or “recent turbulence persists”.
Out of sample: each year is forecast with a model trained only on previous years, as in real conditions.

title: Results: the model versus the benchmark
text:
How to read the charts
Each point is the gap between the factor model and the best model without factors over 2010-2026. The bar is the 99.4% confidence interval, computed by block bootstrap. This level corrects for the 9 comparisons (5% divided by 9).

Above zero, the factor model does better.
It only beats the benchmark if the whole bar is above zero, in both readings.

title: Results: the model versus the benchmark
section: What about forecasting the return directly?
text:
What about forecasting the return directly?
A last attempt, decided after the results and therefore exploratory (protocol, point 13). Instead of the direction, the model forecasts the return over h sessions, that is, the percentage change in price. It is compared with the random walk, which assumes the price does not move, and with the past average of returns. 99% interval, corrected for 5 horizons.


Show the code
g = lire("regression_rendements.csv").rename(columns={"ecart_rmse": "ecart"})
HORIZONS_POS = {h: i for i, h in enumerate(HORIZONS["sens"])}
points_ic(g, {"Raw reading": (g["lecture"] == "brute", SERIE[0]), "Control reading": (g["lecture"] != "brute", SERIE[1])},
          "Return: RMSE gap against the random walk (positive = model better)", "RMSE gap").show()


                            
                                            


The model does significantly worse than the random walk at almost every horizon: the bars lie entirely below zero. It only guesses the sign of the return in 42 to 52% of cases. As the protocol required, no “forecast price curve” is therefore drawn: the best forecast of tomorrow’s price remains today’s price.

title: Impact of weather on production
text:
Why this question
The project showed that the weather does not help forecast the price: the market seems to absorb the information before we do. But a cocoa tree does not read the markets. If rainfall and heat matter, their effect should show directly in the quantities harvested. And since the weather does not depend on production, a measured link between the two can be read, with caution, as a cause-and-effect relationship.

title: Impact of weather on production
text:
The data

Production: tonnes of beans per country and per year, from 1991 to 2024, in the 9 countries tracked (FAOSTAT).
Rainfall: annual CHIRPS total in each country’s cocoa areas, with points weighted by the MapSPAM crop map, from 1991 to 2025.
Temperature: annual mean of daily maximums (NASA POWER), only since 2005.

Why production and not yield? Yield per hectare seemed the natural target. But in Côte d’Ivoire, FAO estimates it itself in 29 years out of 34: it stays frozen around 500 kg/ha. It therefore contains almost no information about the weather. Production, on the other hand, is official in 9 cases out of 10.


Show the code
f = pd.read_csv(RACINE / "data" / "raw" / "t3_offre" / "faostat_cacao.csv")
civ = f[(f["Area"] == "Côte d'Ivoire") & (f["Year"] >= 1991)].pivot(index="Year", columns="Element", values="Value")
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=civ.index, y=civ["Production"] / civ["Production"].iloc[0] * 100, mode="lines", name="Production",
                line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[0]), hovertemplate="%{x}: production %{y:.0f} (1991 = 100)<extra></extra>")
fig.add_scatter(x=civ.index, y=civ["Yield"] / civ["Yield"].iloc[0] * 100, mode="lines", name="Yield per hectare",
                line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[1]), hovertemplate="%{x}: yield %{y:.0f} (1991 = 100)<extra></extra>")
fig.update_layout(title="Côte d'Ivoire: FAOSTAT production and yield, 1991 = 100", height=360,
                  yaxis_title="Index (1991 = 100)")
fig.show()


                            
                                            


Production varies from one year to the next, while the published yield is almost flat: a sign of an estimated value, not a measured one.

title: Impact of weather on production
text:
The method, in plain terms
Each country is compared with itself:

does a year drier or wetter than usual in that country give a harvest below that country’s trend?
shocks that hit all countries in the same year, such as world demand or prices, are removed;
each country’s long-term growth, linked to the expansion of plantations, is removed as well.

Rainfall is measured as deviations from the country’s normal: 0 is a normal year, −1.5 a clearly dry year, +1.5 a clearly wet year. Rainfall in the year and in the previous year are both tested, because harvest calendars do not follow the calendar year. A “squared” term captures the possibility that too much water may be as harmful as too little.
With only 9 countries, the usual tests are too optimistic. We therefore use:

a wild bootstrap: the estimate is redone by randomly flipping the sign of each country’s deviations, over the 512 possible combinations;
a permutation: weather years are shuffled within each country, 2,000 times, to see whether the true link does better than chance.

title: Impact of weather on production
section: Why a null result, and what it would take to go further
text:
Why a null result, and what it would take to go further
A null result does not prove that the weather has no effect. It says that these data do not allow it to be measured. Four likely reasons:

Annual, national rainfall is too coarse. What matters for the cocoa tree is how rain is spread through the year, in particular the length of the dry season, not the total.
FAOSTAT production is imperfect. It is often revised and sometimes taken from other bodies. It does not follow the harvest season, which runs from October to September.
Few independent observations: 9 countries, about 33 years.
Other factors dominate: diseases (swollen shoot), ageing orchards, prices paid to farmers, smuggling between neighbouring countries.

Possible extensions: seasonal indicators (dry-season rainfall, number of deficit days), production data by region or by season (bean arrivals at Ivorian ports, ICCO quarterly figures), and extreme temperatures rather than averages. These analyses would be decided after this first result: they would have to be presented as exploratory.

C. In crisis periods, does attention matter?
The high-volatility regime is defined from the past only: volatility over the last 60 sessions exceeds the 80th percentile of its history. This covers 12.5% of the sessions in 2010-2023, against 95% of those in 2024-2026.
We measure the loss when the investors and biases family (Google Trends, GDELT news, CFTC positions) is removed, separately in each regime.

                    hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>Loss %{{y:+.4f}}<br>99.72% CI: %{{customdata[0]:+.4f}} to %{{customdata[1]:+.4f}}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=MUET, width=1.5, dash="dot"))

                  xaxis=dict(tickvals=list(xpos.values()), ticktext=[etiq[k] for k in cibles]), yaxis_title="Score loss")

Only one case stands out: volatility at 60 sessions in high volatility, where the family helps the model (interval from +0.0004 to +0.0225). SHAP points to the volume of news articles on cocoa (GDELT), almost zero before 2024 and dominant afterwards. Four reasons for caution:

the effect is measured against the model without this family. The full model remains worse than past volatility alone;
media attention probably follows the crisis rather than announcing it;
the effect rests on about 11 independent windows;
the analysis was chosen after seeing the results.

No effect appears on the price direction, at any horizon.

A technical trap. CC=F chains contracts together: when a contract expires, Yahoo switches to the next one, and the price can jump without any real market move, by up to 30% in 2024. The models account for this through a control reading, which removes these jumps (Method page).

Quality of the CC=F series, the models’ target
How Yahoo builds CC=F. CC=F follows a single contract at a time, the front month, then switches to the next. Prices are not spliced (no back-adjustment): at each switch, the price gap between the two contracts shows up as a spurious return.
How the project detects the switches (scripts/03 and src/cacao/grille.py):

Before expiry, Yahoo stays on the expiring contract while trading has already moved to the next one: volume collapses. A roll is detected when volume rises back above 1,000 contracts after 3 sessions below 100.
The jump day is the day with the largest absolute return between that day and the next.
Treatment: no corrected series is published. The models are also judged in the control reading: windows without a roll up to 20 sessions, jump-day return set to zero at 60 and 120 sessions.

Limit: this detection is done after the fact (it uses the next day’s volume and return). It is only used for evaluation, never as a variable.

section: Rainfall in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana
text:
Rainfall in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana
Why rainfall. Cocoa comes mainly from West Africa. Among the 9 countries tracked, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana together account for about half of production (FAOSTAT, weights used in the project). The cocoa tree needs regular rainfall:

a drought reduces flowering and bean size;
excess moisture favours diseases, such as black pod rot.

A poor rainy season can therefore reduce the harvest of the following months, and push the price up if the market had not anticipated it.


Show the code
dernier = part.iloc[-1]
print(f"Weight in the production of the 9 countries tracked ({part.index[-1]}): Côte d'Ivoire {dernier['CIV']:.0%}, Ghana {dernier['GHA']:.0%}, "
      f"Indonesia {dernier['IDN']:.0%}, Ecuador {dernier['ECU']:.0%}.")


Weight in the production of the 9 countries tracked (2026): Côte d'Ivoire 41%, Ghana 11%, Indonesia 14%, Ecuador 9%.


How to read the chart. Each line compares rainfall over the last 3 months with the normal for the same months over 1991-2004. The gap is expressed in standard deviations, a measure of the usual gap from one year to the next.

0: normal rainfall;
+1: clearly more rain than usual;
−1: clearly less;
beyond ±2: rare situation.



Show the code

for i, (pays, nom) in enumerate([("CIV", "Côte d'Ivoire"), ("GHA", "Ghana")]):
    s = d[f"CHIRPS_ANOM3M_{pays}"]
    fig.add_scatter(x=s.index, y=s, mode="lines", name=nom, line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[i]),
                    hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>%{{x|%m/%Y}}: %{{y:.2f}} standard deviations<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hrect(y0=0, y1=6, fillcolor=SERIE[0], opacity=0.04, line_width=0)
fig.add_annotation(x=d.index[60], y=4.6, text="Wetter than normal", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color=ENCRE_2))
fig.add_annotation(x=d.index[60], y=-2.6, text="Drier than normal", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color=ENCRE_2))

fig.update_layout(title="Rainfall over the last 3 months, deviation from normal (source: CHIRPS)", height=400,
                  yaxis=dict(title="Standard deviations", range=[-3, 5.2]))
fig.show()


                            
                                            


What we observe.

The two countries often move together, since they are neighbours.
Early 2026 is far above normal, between +3 and +4.7 standard deviations. Note, however, that December to March is the dry season. Normal rainfall is low then, so a few showers are enough to produce a large deviation.
What the project concludes: these rainfall deviations did not improve the price forecast (Results page). Either the information is already absorbed by the market when it is published, or the effect on the harvest is too indirect to be captured.


Rainfall in millimetres and seasons
A standard deviation does not say how much it rained. The charts below give actual monthly rainfall in cocoa areas (CHIRPS, points weighted by the crop map), compared with its normal.

Hover over a month to see observed rainfall, the normal, the deviation in standard deviations and the season. The models’ standard deviations use the 1991-2004 normal, prior to the sample, so that no future information enters it. The chart shows the 1991-2020 normal, the usual climatological reference, which is easier to read.


From climate to market: what lags?
The assumed chain is long. At each link, the table shows what the project was able to measure.



Step
Assumed lag
What the project measured




1. Climate conditions
Observed to the day; published from 3 days (NASA) to 3-4 weeks (CHIRPS)
Data collected, cross-checked between 3 sources


2. Crop development
Several months between flowering and harvest (agronomic lag not quantified here)
Not measured: no flowering or pod data


3. Yields
Following season
FAOSTAT yield unusable, estimated by FAO (Weather and production page)


4. Production
October-to-September season
No demonstrated effect of annual rainfall (p = 0.16)


5. World supply
Known from market estimates, then from FAOSTAT at N+2
FAOSTAT production: information too late for the market


6. Market reaction
As soon as the information is anticipated
No improvement in out-of-sample forecasts



To look for a lag between rainfall and price, we measure the correlation between the 3-month rainfall deviation, at the time it is published, and the cocoa return over the 3 months starting 0 to 12 months later.


Show the code
dl = lire("climat_delais.csv")
fig = go.Figure()
for k, (p, nom) in enumerate((("CIV", "Côte d'Ivoire"), ("GHA", "Ghana"))):
    x = dl[dl["pays"] == p]
    fig.add_scatter(x=x["delai_mois"] + (k - 0.5) * 0.18, y=x["rho"], mode="markers", name=nom, marker=dict(size=9, color=SERIE[k], line=dict(width=2, color="white")),
                    error_y=dict(type="data", symmetric=False, array=x["ic_haut"] - x["rho"], arrayminus=x["rho"] - x["ic_bas"], color=SERIE[k], thickness=2, width=3),
                    customdata=np.stack([x["delai_mois"], x["ic_bas"], x["ic_haut"]], axis=1),
                    hovertemplate=f"{nom}<br>Lag %{{customdata[0]}} months<br>Correlation %{{y:+.2f}}<br>95% CI: %{{customdata[1]:+.2f}} to %{{customdata[2]:+.2f}}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=MUET, dash="dot"))
fig.update_layout(title="Published rainfall and cocoa return 3 months later, by lag (rank correlation)", height=380,
                  xaxis=dict(title="Lag between rainfall publication and the start of the return window (months)", dtick=1),
                  yaxis_title="Correlation")
fig.show()


                            
                                            



Correlations are weak (−0.07 to +0.19) and almost all compatible with zero.
Only one out of 26 has an interval excluding zero: Ghana at 12 months (+0.17). With 26 trials, such an exception is expected by chance, and it does not survive a multiple-testing correction.
Correlations become slightly positive at 10-12 months: more rain would go with a price rise a year later, the opposite of the intuition “more rain, more supply”. This is a lead, not a result. One hypothesis would be excess moisture and diseases.
Conclusion: no climate lag emerges as usable for forecasting the price with these data. This is consistent with the model results.

title: Data
text:
El Niño
What it is. El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean, recurring roughly every 2 to 7 years. It disrupts the weather in many regions. It is often associated with a more pronounced dry season in West Africa. La Niña is the opposite phenomenon: a cooling of the Pacific.
How to read the chart. NOAA’s ONI index measures the ocean temperature anomaly, in degrees.

Above +0.5 °C: El Niño episode.
Below −0.5 °C: La Niña episode.

According to our data, the strongest episodes since 2005 are those of 2015-2016, with a peak of +2.6 °C, and 2023-2024, with about +2.0 °C. A new strong episode appears in 2026.


Show the code
s = d["ONI"]
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=s.index, y=s, mode="lines", line=dict(width=2, color=SERIE[0]), name="ONI",
                hovertemplate="%{x|%m/%Y}: %{y:+.2f} °C<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hrect(y0=0.5, y1=3, fillcolor=SERIE[1], opacity=0.08, line_width=0)
fig.add_hrect(y0=-3, y1=-0.5, fillcolor=SERIE[0], opacity=0.08, line_width=0)
fig.add_annotation(x=s.index[30], y=2.6, text="El Niño zone (above +0.5 °C)", showarrow=False, font=dict(color=ENCRE_2), xanchor="left")
fig.add_annotation(x=s.index[30], y=-2.6, text="La Niña zone (below −0.5 °C)", showarrow=False, font=dict(color=ENCRE_2), xanchor="left")

                  yaxis=dict(range=[-3, 3], title="°C"))
fig.show()


                            
                                            


What the project concludes: as with rainfall, the El Niño index did not improve the price forecast. Episodes are announced months in advance by weather agencies: the market probably anticipates them.

The 8 factor families
Each family groups variables that tell the same story about the price of cocoa. The model never receives raw levels, such as a price or a rate. It receives changes (over 1, 3 or 6 months depending on the horizon) or deviations from normal, and each data point enters only once published.

NoteClimate: the weather in cocoa areas





Why. The harvest depends on rainfall, heat and humidity. A bad season can reduce supply and push the price up.
Variables, for Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Indonesia and a world index weighted by production:

rainfall over the last 7 and 30 days, deviation from normal (ERA5);
rainfall over the last 1, 3 and 6 months, deviation from normal (CHIRPS);
maximum temperature, air humidity, deep soil moisture, sunshine and wind, as a 30-day deviation from normal (NASA POWER);
El Niño index (ONI) and its change over 3 months.

Weather points are placed in growing areas using the MapSPAM map.









NoteGeopolitics: tensions and conflicts





Why. A political crisis in a producing country can block exports. In 2011, Alassane Ouattara called for the suspension of Ivorian exports during the post-election crisis.
Variables:

for Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Indonesia: the country’s share of world news, the share of conflict events and the share of protests, over 30 days (GDELT event database);
global geopolitical risk index (GPR): overall level, acts and threats, as a moving average;
monthly GPR index by country, for Brazil, Indonesia and Peru. It does not exist for Côte d’Ivoire or Ghana.










NoteBiodiversity: soils, forests and inputs





Why. Soil depletion, deforestation and the use of fertilisers or pesticides weigh on yields in the medium term.
Variables, for Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Indonesia:

vegetation fires detected by satellite in cocoa areas, 30-day deviation from normal (NASA FIRMS);
pesticide and nitrogen use per cultivated hectare, annual change (FAOSTAT);
cocoa yield per hectare, annual change (FAOSTAT). Often estimated by FAO, see the Weather and production page.

FAOSTAT data for a given year are only used from 1 January of year N+2, their approximate publication date. Diseases (swollen shoot) and illegal gold mining have no public series: they are missing.









NoteProduction costs: energy, fertilisers, currencies





Why. Producing, transporting and exporting cost more when energy or fertilisers rise. The currencies of producing countries also change what farmers and exporters earn.
Variables:

oil (WTI) and natural gas, as changes;
world prices of urea, DAP, TSP and potash, change over 1 and 3 months (World Bank);
exchange rates against the dollar of the euro, the Ghanaian cedi, the Indonesian rupiah and the Nigerian naira, as changes. Côte d’Ivoire uses the CFA franc, pegged to the euro.










NoteProduction and supply: the quantities harvested





Why. It is the most direct fundamental: less cocoa harvested should mean a higher price.
Variables: bean production in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Indonesia, annual change (FAOSTAT), available at N+2. It is the smallest family. Stocks data are missing: ICE certified stocks are paid.









NoteMarket and finance: cocoa itself and its context





Why. The recent past of the price (trend, turbulence, volume traded) and the financial context (dollar, interest rates) influence the decisions of buyers and speculators.
Variables:

past cocoa return over 1 and 3 months, recent volatility and volume traded, as a deviation from its usual level;
dollar index, as a change;
US 10-year and 3-month rates, as changes.

This is the information that models without factors already exploit.









NoteInvestors and biases: speculation and attention





Why. Funds can amplify moves when they buy or sell en masse. Strong public or media attention can accompany excesses.
Variables:

net positions of funds, non-commercials and producers, as a share of open interest, and their changes. Open interest as a change (weekly CFTC reports, used after their Friday publication);
Google searches for “chocolate”, “cocoa” and “cocoa price”, change over 1 month and over 1 year;
volume and tone of news articles on cocoa, worldwide and in West Africa, as a moving average (GDELT).










NoteDemand and substitutes: buyers and related products





Why. Chocolate makers are the final buyers. Sugar, palm oil and coffee are grown in the same regions or go into the same products.
Variables:

share prices of Barry Callebaut, Hershey, Mondelez, Nestlé and Lindt (two securities), as returns;
world prices of sugar, palm oil and robusta coffee, change over 1 and 3 months (World Bank).

The model is re-estimated without one family, then the loss of out-of-sample performance is measured.

Positive (red): the family was helping the model.
Negative (blue): the model is better without it.
An asterisk marks a 99.4% interval that excludes zero.

title: Factor families
text:
Why the two measures diverge
SHAP gives climate 18 to 27% of contributions for the price direction. The removal test shows, however, that these contributions do not help out of sample. Three reasons:

SHAP measures use, not usefulness. It says which variables the model relies on, not whether that reliance improves the forecast.
Families differ in size. Climate has more than 40 variables. A sum of contributions favours large families.
Families are correlated. The model can spread the same signal across several families.

This is the disagreement anticipated in point 7 of the protocol, and a good methodological lesson: a large SHAP share does not prove that a variable is useful.

title: Which factor weighs most on the price of cocoa?
text:
The question
In 2024 cocoa went through a historic crisis: the futures contract passed 10,000 dollars per tonne for the first time on 26 March 2024 (Bloomberg). This project asks which family of factors brings the most information for forecasting cocoa, out of sample:

the direction of the price over 1, 5, 20, 60 and 120 sessions;
its volatility over 5, 20, 60 and 120 sessions.

Eight families are tested: climate, geopolitics, biodiversity, production costs, production and supply, market and finance, investors and biases, demand and substitutes.

title: Which factor weighs most on the price of cocoa?
text:
Takeaways

The past price already contains the information. What public factors say is already in the price at the time of the forecast. The market seems to absorb available information quickly.
Volatility is predictable, but from its own past. Turbulent periods last. A model that only looks at past volatility (HAR) beats the factor model at every horizon.
SHAP can mislead. It attributes 18 to 27% of contributions to climate for the price direction. Yet removing climate does not worsen the forecasts, and even improves them at 60 sessions (Families page).
A single lead, exploratory: in crisis periods, the volume of news articles on cocoa helps the model forecast volatility at 60 sessions. The model nonetheless remains worse than past volatility alone (Exploratory leads page).

title: Method and limits
text:
Limits

Contract rolls. CC=F switches contracts: the price jumps, up to 30% in 2024, are detected after the fact. The control reading handles them, without removing them.
Few independent long-horizon observations. About 70 independent windows at 60 sessions and 35 at 120 sessions over 2010-2026.
Revised data. FAOSTAT is taken in its current vintage, not the one known at the time. The 2005-2019 GEFS reforecasts were produced after the fact.
Imperfect weather sources. NASA rainfall has a wet bias in 2020-2023, and ERA5 drifts against CHIRPS in West Africa. The GEFS temperature correction inherits the NASA bias.
Publication lags partly assumed (FIRMS, ONI, Google Trends).
Missing data. No stocks series: ICE certified stocks are paid, or available through Bloomberg. Nothing either on soil poisoning, swollen shoot or illegal gold mining. 2026 fires are missing.
Price only. The conclusion concerns forecasting price and volatility, not the causal effect of the factors on production.
